summary: Records the considerations reached by the IETF NVO3 Working Group, starting from its encapsulation Design Team, for a common encapsulation for network virtualization overlays. It is a record for future discussions. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Different virtual networks wrap their packets differently. This records what the group learned when thinking about one common wrapping.

subtitle: How the IETF chose a common way to wrap packets for virtual networks.

tldr.problem: Different network virtualization technologies wrap packets in different ways, making operations and hardware support complex when multiple encapsulations coexist.
tldr.mechanism: The NVO3 Working Group evaluated three encapsulation candidates (Geneve, GUE, and VXLAN-GPE), weighing hardware implementability, extensibility, and operational concerns.
tldr.outcome: The group recommended Geneve as the common encapsulation for network virtualization, with suggested enhancements to support security, telemetry, and other extensions.

today: RFC 9638 is an Informational specification that has not been obsoleted. It documents the consensus of the IETF NVO3 Working Group and provides implementation guidance. Geneve has become the de facto standard for network virtualization overlays, with deployments in production cloud infrastructure and continued development of security and telemetry extensions.

sections.title: The Encapsulation Problem
sections.content: Network virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) overlays virtual networks on top of physical IP networks by wrapping packets in encapsulation headers. Different encapsulation formats introduce challenges: different formats coexisting in a single data center mean operations staff must manage multiple technologies, and hardware vendors struggle to efficiently implement several options. The IETF NVO3 Working Group was chartered to settle on a common encapsulation to maximize interoperability and simplify both hardware and software implementations.
sections.eli5: Multiple ways to wrap packets in a data center mean routers and switches need to handle them all, which costs money and creates headaches.

sections.title: Three Candidates Compared
sections.content:
Geneve uses a flexible, variable-length header with Type-Length-Value (TLV) extensions, allowing operators to add new fields without changing the protocol. Its critical bit makes it easy for endpoints to decide whether unknown options must be processed or can be ignored. The header includes a length field so hardware can skip over options efficiently.

GUE (Generic UDP Encapsulation) uses a smaller base header with a fixed set of flag-based extensions. This simplifies parsing in some ways but is less flexible: new extensions require guessing which ones will be widely used early, and adding new options later becomes difficult.

VXLAN-GPE (Virtual eXtensible LAN with Generic Protocol Extension) extends the standard VXLAN format minimally. However, it lacks built-in extensibility and does not include a header length field, making it harder for hardware to skip over options or for transit devices to read the inner packet.
sections.eli5: Geneve is like a container with labeled compartments you can add; GUE is pre-built with fixed slots; VXLAN-GPE is the smallest but hardest to extend.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.content:
The group considered several practical constraints. Hardware implementations need to efficiently skip the encapsulation header to find the inner packet for TCP offload and policy processing. Extensions are inevitable: telemetry needs in-band metadata, security requires header authentication and payload encryption, and group-based policy carries tenant context. Extensions can be added via TLVs (flexible but harder to parse) or bit flags (simpler but inflexible).

A control plane can manage complexity by having endpoints advertise which extensions they support and in what order, allowing hardware to handle a smaller subset than what might exist in the full standard. This shifts some burden from hardware to software management, which is practical since most hardware implementations handle only a subset of all possible features anyway.
sections.eli5: Routers need to quickly find the actual data inside the wrapper, but sometimes need to read special fields along the way. A smart control system can tell each router which special fields to expect.

sections.title: Security and Extensibility
sections.content:
A critical insight is that encapsulation headers must be protected. A single bit flip in the Virtual Network Identifier (VNI) could deliver a packet to the wrong tenant. Extensions using HMAC can authenticate headers and outer IP addresses, preventing VNI spoofing. Payload encryption via DTLS or IPsec-ESP extensions provides tenant data privacy while keeping the NVO3 header readable by network elements.

The encapsulation must support multiple extensions coexisting on a single UDP port, avoiding the need to define new well-known ports for each new capability. TLVs are self-describing (all information is in the TLV itself) and allow different software modules to process different extensions without conflict, which is valuable in multi-vendor environments.
sections.eli5: Virtual packets need locks so bad actors cannot forge or snoop them. Extensions let you add different kinds of locks without breaking existing systems.

sections.title: Why Geneve Won
sections.content:
Geneve was chosen because it balances flexibility with hardware reality. The 24-bit VNI matches existing VXLAN and NVGRE deployments, reducing the need to renumber virtual networks. The length field lets hardware skip options, and the critical bit lets endpoints distinguish mandatory from optional extensions. TLVs offer better hardware modularity than bit flags: fields describe themselves, so hardware does not need separate tables to learn the size of each extension.

Real deployments of Geneve with TLV extensions already exist in production (in Open vSwitch and other virtualization platforms), and new hardware supports Geneve option parsing. The RFC recommends that Geneve documents be updated to clarify how control planes can negotiate extension subsets and ordering, and to define well-known secure option TLVs for header integrity and payload encryption.
sections.eli5: Geneve works because it is not too simple and not too complex, scales from software to hardware, and people are already using it.
